title: First-order diagonal restriction is determined by the two axes
statement: Let $S$ be any scheme [def-pc-scheme] and let $D=S[\varepsilon]$ be its dual-number thickening [def-sc-dual-numbers] over $S$. Let $X$ be any scheme over $S$ and $f,g:D\times_S D\to X$ be $S$-morphisms. Let $z:D\to D$ be the projection to $S$ followed by the zero section $S\to D$. If $f\circ(\mathrm{id},z)=g\circ(\mathrm{id},z)$ and $f\circ(z,\mathrm{id})=g\circ(z,\mathrm{id})$, then $f\circ(\mathrm{id},\mathrm{id})=g\circ(\mathrm{id},\mathrm{id})$.

source.place: Lemma 33.16.2 proof: square-zero pushout and epsilon_i mapping to epsilon; local arbitrary-ring form and group-unit-law application written out here

proof.text: Locally on an affine open Spec R of the base, the product of dual-number thickenings is Spec A for A=R[epsilon,delta]/(epsilon^2,delta^2). Its underlying space and those of both axes and the diagonal identify with Spec R, since the nilpotent ideals lie in every prime. Equality on either axis therefore identifies the underlying maps of f and g. Around every image point restrict to an affine target open, and shrink the affine base open inside its inverse image.

The two ring maps now agree modulo (delta) and modulo (epsilon). For each element of the target coordinate ring their difference lies in the intersection of these ideals. The unique expansion a+b epsilon+c delta+d epsilon delta shows that this intersection is exactly (epsilon delta), even if R is nonreduced or has zero divisors.

The diagonal ring map sends epsilon and delta to the same square-zero variable, so annihilates (epsilon delta). The diagonal comorphisms therefore agree. Scheme morphisms glue uniquely over an open cover of the source; hence the diagonal scheme maps, and thus the slice morphisms over S, agree globally.
